Probably not reliably—though it may be possible with excellent conditions and an unobstructed horizon.

The Moon is only **6.5° above the eastern-southeastern horizon** (azimuth **101.5°**) and is a very thin **3.95%-illuminated crescent**. Since the Sun is just **1.3° below the horizon**, you are still in **civil twilight**, so the sky is bright while the crescent is faint. The Moon–Sun separation of **22.9°** gives it a reasonable elongation, but the low altitude and thin phase make visibility difficult.

Your best chance is to look toward **east-southeast**, about 6–7° above a completely unobstructed horizon—roughly the width of three fingers held at arm’s length. Avoid trees, hills, buildings, haze, and bright local lights. Binoculars would make it much easier, but use them only after locating the Sun’s position safely and never scan near the Sun.

So: **a sharp-eyed observer might glimpse it, especially from a dark, clear coastal viewpoint, but an unaided-eye sighting is unlikely and not guaranteed.** It should become easier as the Moon rises, but the sky will also brighten rapidly after sunrise.
